questions.prompt: A domino covers exactly two squares that share a side. A tiling covers every square of the region exactly once, with no domino hanging off the region. One square is removed from a 5 by 5 board, and the other 24 squares are to be tiled by 12 dominoes. Rows and columns are numbered 1 to 5. Give the row r and column c of a square whose removal makes a tiling possible.
questions.rule: isInteger(r) and isInteger(c) and r >= 1 and r <= 5 and c >= 1 and c <= 5 and isEven(r + c)
questions.correct_answer: any values that satisfy: isInteger(r) and isInteger(c) and r >= 1 and r <= 5 and c >= 1 and c <= 5 and isEven(r + c) (example: r = 1, c = 1)

questions.prompt: An L-tromino is three squares in an L shape (a 2 by 2 square with one square missing). It may be turned any way. In how many ways can a rectangle 2 squares tall and 3 wide be tiled by two L-trominoes?

sections.skill: Strategy: color the board like a checkerboard
sections.relationship: Students try placements forever on a region that cannot be tiled. Counting colors can prove impossibility at once, and shows when a search is still needed.
sections.author_note: Students try placements forever on a region that cannot be tiled. Counting colors can prove impossibility at once, and shows when a search is still needed.

lesson.title: Color the board like a checkerboard
text: Color the squares in a checkerboard pattern: squares that share a side get different colors.
Every domino covers one dark and one light square. So a region can be tiled only if it has equally many dark and light squares.
Equal counts do not guarantee a tiling. Then look for a square with only one neighbor: its domino is forced.

example.title: Worked example (a different region)
prompt: A T shape: three squares in a row, plus one square below the middle one. Can it be tiled by 2 dominoes?
steps: Colors: the middle square is dark; the two ends and the square below are light. That is 1 dark and 3 light.
Each domino needs one dark square, so at most one domino fits. No tiling exists.

questions.prompt: A 4 by 4 board is colored like a checkerboard. How many of its squares are dark?
Every domino placed on a checkerboard covers one dark square and one light square.

A domino covers exactly two squares that share a side. A tiling covers every square of the region exactly once, with no domino hanging off the region. A region has 7 dark and 5 light squares on a checkerboard coloring. According to the color count, what is the greatest number of dominoes that could be placed on it without overlapping?

A domino covers exactly two squares that share a side. A tiling covers every square of the region exactly once, with no domino hanging off the region. A region has 6 dark and 6 light squares. What does the color count tell you?

choices.text: It can be tiled in exactly 6 ways.
It can certainly be tiled by 6 dominoes.
It does not rule out a tiling; you still have to find one or show none exists.
It cannot be tiled by dominoes.

questions.correct_answer: It does not rule out a tiling; you still have to find one or show none exists.

A straight tromino covers three squares in a row. A 3 by 3 square can be tiled by three straight trominoes in exactly 2 ways.
A straight tromino covers three squares in a row, flat or upright. One corner square is removed from a 4 by 4 board. Can the other 15 squares be tiled by 5 straight trominoes?

choices.text: Yes, and there is more than one way.
No: the corner gap blocks every tiling.
No: 15 squares cannot be split into trominoes.
Yes, but in exactly one way.

questions.correct_answer: Yes, and there is more than one way.

questions.correct_answer: any values that satisfy: n == 5 (example: n = 5)
